the question: When is the marginal distribution of a set of variables in a multidimensional contingency table equal to the marginal distribution of another set of variables in the same table? We present necessary and sufficient conditions under which this is the case.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Whittemore's notion is a very useful concept in the study of multidimensional contingency tables.
collapsibility as originally defined by Bishop et al. is a special case of collapsibility as defined and developed by Whittemore.
collapsibility as described in this article is a property of a hierarchical log linear models which is useful for interpretation of the model and formulation of hypotheses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

collapsibility of a hierarchical log linear models is a necessary condition for the marginal distributions associated with the model to be independent of the marginal distributions associated the model.
collapsibility is a very useful tool for the analysis of multidimensional contingency tables.
Whittemore's (1978) notion of collapsibility is the most appropriate for multidimensional contingency tables and is the most useful in facilitating interpretation of hierarchical log linear models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Whittemore's definition of collapsibility is the appropriate one for hierarchical models.
collapsibility is not a binary property of a log linear model, but rather a property of a model relative to a particular partitioning of the variables in the model.
collapsibility as discussed by Whittemore and Asmussen & Edward is a very powerful tool for understanding hierarchical log linear models.
